html:
The Suquamish are a Lushootseed-speaking Coast Salish people of the Kitsap Peninsula, on the west side of Puget Sound in Washington, across the water from today's Seattle. They lived in large cedar plank houses and fished for salmon.

Their winter town at Agate Passage had the Old Man House, one of the largest longhouses on the coast, well over a hundred metres long. The leader Si'ahl, known as Chief Seattle, was Suquamish on his father's side and Duwamish through his mother; the city of Seattle is named after him. He signed the Treaty of Point Elliott in 1855, which set aside the Port Madison Reservation for the Suquamish. US agents burned Old Man House around 1870 to push families into single homes. Their neighbours include the Duwamish across the sound, and they are part of the wider Coast Salish world.
